title: Refinery margins watch
dek: Crack spreads, utilization, and turnarounds: how refinery economics set the bid for discounted heavy barrels like Western Canadian Select (WCS).

claims.text: A crack spread measures the difference between the purchase price of crude oil and the selling price of finished products, such as gasoline and distillate fuel, that a refinery produces from the crude. It is an indicator of the short-term profit margin of refineries, but it excludes other variable costs and all fixed costs.
claims.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

claims.text: The 3-2-1 spread approximates the product yield at a typical US refinery: for every three barrels of crude oil processed, the refinery makes two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillate fuel.
claims.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

claims.text: The calculation: add the spot price for two barrels of gasoline to one barrel of diesel (multiplying per-gallon quotes by 42 gallons per barrel), subtract the price of three barrels of crude, and divide by three to get a spread in dollars per barrel.
claims.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

claims.text: The 3-2-1 crack spread is the most widely used benchmark for US refiner profitability. It is traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), where refiners use it as a hedging instrument to lock in their margins.

Forbes columnist Robert Rapier's third-quarter review found refiners leading energy stocks: Marathon Petroleum returned 55.1 percent in the quarter, Phillips 66 gained 51.8 percent, and Valero returned 49.4 percent, with smaller independents PBF Energy up nearly 70 percent and CVR Energy up almost 86 percent. Rapier argues refining capacity, not crude availability, has increasingly become the constraint, as disruptions to Russian and Middle Eastern refining capacity widened crack spreads. He cautions that refining is notoriously cyclical and unusually high margins can disappear as disrupted capacity returns.

CNBC reported Goldman Sachs expects global diesel and jet-fuel crack spreads to average above $40 a barrel in 2027, more than twice their usual level of around $20, even as the bank expects Brent crude to stabilize near $80 a barrel as Hormuz flows normalize. The bank's Nikhil Bhandari said product prices must stay high enough to keep some demand destruction going into next year, warning that any 2027 demand rebound would push the global refining system to its highest utilization in two decades. CLSA's Baden Moore added that underlying product demand remains intact and that rebuilding inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years.

Reuters reported the IEA's governing board is expected to decide the details of the G7's 100-million-barrel diesel and crude emergency release at an October 14-15 board meeting, after the October 3 G7 announcement gave no breakdown of crude versus diesel volumes, no participating countries, and no timeline. Italy would take part, one source said, and the EU's oil coordination group was set to meet October 7. The article notes the Iran war already triggered the biggest emergency release on record, 400 million barrels, in March, also coordinated by the IEA, and that oil prices fell more than $2 on October 6 as rising Middle Eastern exports and the G7 release eased supply concerns.

The EIA's third-quarter wrap put US refineries at unseasonally high levels in 3Q26, with utilization averaging 95 percent and plants processing the most crude oil for a third quarter since 2019, when refining capacity was 4 percent higher. The agency reported the quarterly average gasoline crack spread more than doubled its year-ago level despite fading in the second half of the quarter, while the distillate and jet-fuel crack spreads almost tripled theirs on tight global supply. In the week ending September 25, US distillate inventories sat 13 percent below their five-year average, gasoline 7 percent below, and jet fuel 3 percent above.

RBN Energy's daily 3-2-1 crack print stood at $64.65 a barrel on Oct 4, down $2.74 on the day, continuing the cool-off from the $73.12 near-record reading of Sep 22 and the $68.19 print of Sep 27 already on record.

China removed a swing supplier from the product market: Beijing did not authorize October fuel exports beyond Hong Kong and Macau, and state major PetroChina canceled some gasoline and jet cargoes already committed, per Reuters sources reported by OilPrice.com on Oct 1. Chinese refiners had exported 6.01 million tons of products in August, up 12.7 percent year on year, before the curbs; with domestic gasoline and diesel inventories at multi-year lows, refiners are prioritizing the home market.

The diesel-margin turn is dated: the ICE gasoil crack fell to about $70 a barrel on Oct 5 from as high as $85 in the middle of last week, after the G7 announced a release of up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency stocks over the next four months and the risk of a US diesel export ban receded, according to ING head of commodities strategy Warren Patterson. Patterson said the release only brings short-term relief, with diesel margins still historically high because the underlying middle-distillate tightness is unresolved.

The Trading Economics Crack Spread index, which tracks the spread between crude oil and refined products at the average US refinery, surged to a record 75 dollars a barrel in September 2026, up nearly 200 percent since mid-February. The report ties the spike to disrupted Middle East crude exports that pushed US refiners to run above 100 percent of nameplate capacity, and says the presidential administration weighed a ban on diesel exports as domestic gasoline and diesel prices climbed.

The 3-2-1 crack spread stood at 73.12 dollars a barrel on Sep 22, about 3.7 percent below the May 13, 2022 record of 75.89 and far above the post-2006 median near 19 dollars. The benchmark is a gross spot margin before operating costs, Renewable Identification Number (RIN) costs, transport, and refinery-specific yields, and refiners' reported margins lag it by roughly a quarter. RBN Energy's daily print had the spread at 68.19 dollars on Sep 27, showing it cooling off the record but still near triple the median.
claims.source: thetrading.tools (computed from EIA daily spot prices)

claims.text: US gasoline futures held above 3.45 dollars a gallon on Sep 23, the highest since May 21, as the crack spread hit record highs and refiners shifted output toward higher-priced diesel ahead of winter, tightening gasoline supply. The note also cites continued Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refining and reports that Russia is set to extend its diesel export ban beyond September.

On July 17, 2026, the 3-2-1 crack spread closed at $69.66 per barrel, a record high for the third consecutive session. Diesel, the biggest portion of global oil consumption, was the primary driver. US diesel stockpiles were just over 102 million barrels, nearly 11 million below the February 27 level and about 8 million below the five-year seasonal average, per US Energy Information Administration (EIA) data.

The West Texas Intermediate (WTI) 3-2-1 crack spread hit $59 per barrel in August 2026, nearly triple its January level and the highest since the 2020 pandemic crash. The 2010 to 2021 average was about $19 per barrel. The six-month forward curve was pricing about $44, still 35% above the long-run average.

The diesel crack crossed $100 per barrel in August. Gasoline refining margins were $45 to $50 per barrel and jet kerosene $70 to $75, per BloombergNEF data. Diesel effectively left its historical range.

By September 24, the gasoline-over-crude margin had widened to about $58 per barrel, more than triple the 20-year median of $17 and in the 99.8th percentile of every trading day since 2006. US refinery utilization hit 97.4% in late August, the highest since 2018.

The spike's drivers: the Iran war disrupted Middle East product exports, Russia restricted diesel exports, Ukrainian drone strikes hit 21 of Russia's 38 large refineries, and US refiners became the supplier of last resort, pushing fuel exports to record highs while domestic stockpiles drained.
claims.source: Reuters (via BOE Report); Real Investment Advice

claims.text: For the week ended October 2, Reuters reported EIA data showing US refinery crude runs rose by 223,000 barrels a day and utilization ticked up 0.2 points to 92.7 percent. US crude stocks fell 3.2 million barrels to 424.1 million against expectations for a build, on exports jumping 1.2 million barrels a day to 4.77 million. Gasoline stocks rose 0.4 million to 204.7 million, with Gulf Coast gasoline at its lowest since September 2017 and Midwest inventories at a record low; distillate stockpiles, including diesel and heating oil, were little changed at 105.1 million barrels versus an expected 2.1-million-barrel draw.
claims.vintage: Week ending Oct 2, 2026; published Oct 7, 2026; accessed 2026-10-12

claims.text: ExxonMobil entered Friday, September 18 with its 275,000 barrel-per-day Joliet, Illinois refinery still shut, roughly a week after the September 13 power outage and a subsequent flood that overwhelmed a pump, with no firm restart timetable given. The plant produces about 11 million gallons of gasoline and diesel per day and accounts for roughly 6 percent of Midwest refining capacity, making each extra offline day a material hole in regional supply.

Several units at ExxonMobil's Joliet refinery returned to service on Wednesday, Sep 23, starting the restart of the full plant after the September 13 site-wide shutdown, and the refinery was reported back in service around Sep 27. Detail sits behind a paywall; the restart arc is confirmed by the publisher's own headlines and the public restart sequence.

In August, US refinery utilization was 97.4% nationally and 101.8% in the Midwest (PADD 2, the Petroleum Administration for Defense District covering the Midwest), per EIA and BloombergNEF data. Readings above 100% reflect the EIA measuring gross input against nominal operable capacity, with debottlenecking pushing actual throughput above it.
claims.source: Seven Gates Research (citing EIA and BloombergNEF)

claims.text: For the week ending September 18, 2026, US refiners processed less crude, and it was not seasonal maintenance: Exxon's Joliet refinery had been mostly offline since the prior Sunday after a power outage, with floodwater also an issue. The plant accounts for 6 to 8% of regional refining capacity, and the PADD 2 utilization drop pressured an already tight Midwest product market.
claims.source: Tim Dallinger (EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report summary)

claims.text: That same week, US gasoline inventories were about 6% below the five-year seasonal average and distillate about 12% below. Simple cracks moved back toward record high rates.
claims.source: Tim Dallinger (EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report summary)

claims.text: Marathon Petroleum's Q2 2026 refining margin more than doubled to $36.33 per barrel from $17.58 a year earlier, on higher crack spreads across all operating regions. Its refineries ran at 94% of capacity with 2.9 million barrels per day of throughput. The Mid-Continent regional margin was $33.68 per barrel.

Oil Sands Magazine's Sep 30 third-quarter wrap puts the WCS discount topping $20 a barrel in September, the widest since December 2023, and attributes the jump to the unplanned ExxonMobil Joliet outage and a planned maintenance turnaround at BP's 440,000 b/d Whiting refinery in Indiana, which it calls the largest buyer of Alberta's diluted bitumen.

The Western Canadian Select (WCS) discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) stood at 21 dollars a barrel on Sep 21, per Argus market reporting, an unusually wide differential for 2026. With Friday's WTI settlement at 92.44 dollars, implied WCS was 71.44 dollars a barrel, down about 7.09 dollars on the week. Goldman Sachs' fourth-quarter 2026 Brent target of 85 dollars a barrel translates to WCS near 59 dollars, roughly 12.44 dollars below the current implied level.
claims.source: Oil Authority (citing Argus and Goldman Sachs)

claims.text: Midwest refiners invested billions of dollars in coking units to turn Canadian heavy crude into gasoline and diesel. BP's 430,000 barrel-per-day Whiting, Indiana refinery can process up to 85% heavy crude, up from 20% before the upgrades. That conversion hardware is the structural bid under WCS.

The flip side: when Whiting shut down on a transformer failure in February 2024, the WCS discount to WTI widened from $18.10 to $19.00 per barrel on brokerage marks in a single session, on fears of lost heavy-crude demand. Midwest refinery demand is the marginal bid under the barrel.

The same mechanism showed up in September 2026: with Exxon's Joliet refinery offline after a power outage, US refiners processed less crude and Canadian crude imports fell the most week on week. When Midwest runs drop, Canadian barrels are the first to feel it.
claims.source: Tim Dallinger (EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report summary)

claims.text: Competing heavy barrels are getting cheaper at the margin: Vitol and Trafigura, the trading houses marketing Venezuelan crude under the US-controlled export regime, were bidding Brent minus $18 to $20 a barrel for Merey cargoes bound for the US and Europe in late September, seeking steeper discounts as record tanker rates squeezed their margins. The two houses together moved about 597,000 barrels a day in August, more than half of Venezuela's roughly 1.17 million b/d of exports. A discounted Merey offer competes directly with WCS for the same Gulf Coast coker slots.

The competing barrel is a true substitute: Merey 16 runs about 16 degrees API with 2.5 to 2.7 percent sulfur, against WCS at about 21 degrees API and 3.5 percent sulfur. Merey is heavier but slightly less sour; both are delayed-coker feeds, and Merey is the grade US Gulf Coast coking refineries were built to run.
claims.source: Oil & Gas Journal (Merey assay); FuelBridge Merey 16 datasheet, Paraguaná lab Apr 2025; Oil Sands Magazine (WCS spec)

claims.text: The displacement is showing up in US import data: US imports of Venezuelan crude ran 583,000 to 782,000 barrels a day in the two weeks to September 18, landing directly into PADD 3. One syndicated market report put the WCS Houston discount more than $3 a barrel wider since the January announcement as refiners opted for cheaper Venezuelan barrels. Treat that figure as reported, not verified; the checkable version is the ICE ARV - TMW spread.
claims.source: EIA WPSR Table 8 (via local pipeline); marketminute syndicated report Jan 22, 2026 (secondary)

claims.text: Russia is set to extend its ban on most diesel exports beyond the end of September as Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries continue, with an extension of a month or more under consideration, according to people familiar with the matter. The move is cross-verified: the Russian business daily Vedomosti reported on Sep 16 that the ban would run to October 31, citing delayed refinery maintenance and the need to rebuild winter fuel reserves, and Energy Intelligence reported on Sep 18 that an October extension was likely.

Imperial Oil scheduled full turnarounds at two Canadian refineries in 2026: the 197,000 barrel-per-day Strathcona refinery near Edmonton in Q2, and the 124,000 barrel-per-day Sarnia refinery in Q3 and Q4.
claims.source: Oil and Gas Journal (citing Imperial Oil 2026 guidance)

claims.text: Irving Oil's 320,000 barrel-per-day Saint John, New Brunswick refinery, Canada's largest, began a two-month turnaround in September 2026 running to mid-November, an extended maintenance window over its historical 30 to 35 day turnarounds.

US refinery maintenance typically peaks in October, but shipbroker Gibson reported very little confirmed for autumn 2026 because robust margins kept refiners from taking units offline. US utilization was 97.4%, the highest since 2018. The only confirmed PADD 3 turnaround was Exxon's Beaumont fluid catalytic cracker (FCC) and hydrotreaters for about 45 days from early December to mid-January.

Gulf Coast plants ran so hard in the first half of 2026 that deferred work accumulated: catalyst replacements, heat exchanger cleaning, and inspections all compressed into the September to November window. Facilities that ran the most Venezuelan heavy crude face heavier than normal coker and hydrocracker maintenance.
